title: A strongly acidic spill after incomplete neutralization
stem:
A spill contains $20.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.150\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ HCl. It is mixed with $30.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.0800\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ NaOH. Both are fully dissociated. The diagram represents the acid-to-alkali mole ratio; each filled circle represents the same amount of the specified ion. Volumes are additive.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

Unless specified otherwise, use 298 K, $K_w=1.00\times10^{-14}$ and ideal dilute-solution assumptions.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the net ionic neutralization equation and determine the amount of excess reactant.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the pH after mixing. Explain why averaging the original pH values is chemically invalid.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The mixture is diluted to a total volume of 250 cubic centimetres. Find the new pH and explain which quantity is unchanged.

steps.text: $\mathrm{H^+(aq)+OH^-(aq)\rightarrow H_2O(l)}$.
$0.000600$ mol of acid remains.
Neutralization consumes ions; pH is logarithmic and is not an additive conserved quantity.
The excess amount of acid remains 0.000600 mol; dilution changes its concentration.

title: Locating equivalence without confusing an end point
stem:
A $25.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ sample of a fully dissociated monoprotic acid is titrated with $0.100\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ NaOH. The pH curve has its steepest region centred at $18.40\ \mathrm{cm^3}$. A student records an indicator end point at $18.60\ \mathrm{cm^3}$.

title: One ion can either donate or accept a proton
stem:
The hydrogen carbonate ion is shown with its oxygen-bound proton. In separate experiments it is placed in strongly acidic solution and strongly basic solution. A third hydrogen carbonate solution has measured pH 8.20. Do not assume a hydrolysis constant or calculate an equilibrium composition.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

Unless specified otherwise, use 298 K, $K_w=1.00\times10^{-14}$ and ideal dilute-solution assumptions.

parts.prompt: Write one equation in which hydrogen carbonate accepts a proton from H3O+ and another in which it donates a proton to OH−.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the conjugate acid and conjugate base of HCO3−. Explain why carbonate cannot act as a Brønsted–Lowry acid by proton donation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find [H+] and [OH−] in the measured solution and classify it using the ion concentrations.

steps.text: $\mathrm{HCO_3^-+H_3O^+\rightarrow H_2CO_3+H_2O}$.
$\mathrm{HCO_3^-+OH^-\rightarrow CO_3^{2-}+H_2O}$.
Both equations conserve atoms and charge; hydrogen carbonate acts as a base in the first and as an acid in the second.
Conjugate acid $\mathrm{H_2CO_3}$; conjugate base $\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}$.
Conjugate partners differ by exactly one proton and one charge unit.
Carbonate has no proton to donate, although it can accept one.
It is basic because hydroxide concentration exceeds hydrogen-ion concentration.

title: An acid can be concentrated yet weak
stem:
Acid X is monoprotic, concentration $0.0200\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$, pH 1.70. Acid Y is monoprotic, concentration $0.200\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$, pH 2.70. Their measured conductivities under identical conditions are 8.1 and 0.85 mS cm−1 respectively. The graph shows a tenfold dilution of X. No dissociation constant is required.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

Unless specified otherwise, use 298 K, $K_w=1.00\times10^{-14}$ and ideal dilute-solution assumptions.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate [H+] for each acid and the approximate fraction of Y molecules that have dissociated. Neglect water autoionization.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the distinction between acid strength and concentration, using both experiments as evidence.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict the pH of X after the illustrated dilution. Explain why a one-unit rise cannot automatically be assigned to Y after the same dilution.

steps.text: $0.0200$ and $0.00200\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$, respectively.
Fraction for Y $=10^{-2.70}/0.200=0.00998$, approximately $1.00\%$.
Concentration counts total acid amount per volume; strength describes the extent of ionization.
X is essentially completely ionized while only about 1% of Y is ionized despite Y’s tenfold larger total concentration.
The lower measured conductivity of Y is consistent with fewer mobile ions, although mobilities also affect a conductivity comparison.
For fully ionized X, a tenfold dilution divides [H+] by ten.
X changes from pH 1.70 to 2.700.
A weak acid’s ionization equilibrium shifts on dilution, so its fraction dissociated increases and [H+] does not generally fall tenfold.

title: A carbonate impurity measured by back titration
stem:
A $1.000$ g antacid sample contains CaCO3 and an inert, acid-insoluble filler. It is treated with $25.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $1.000\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ HCl. After reaction and removal of dissolved CO2, excess acid requires $20.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.5000\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ NaOH. Use $M_r(\mathrm{CaCO_3})=100.09$. Gas molar volume under collection conditions is $24.8\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}}$.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

Unless specified otherwise, use 298 K, $K_w=1.00\times10^{-14}$ and ideal dilute-solution assumptions.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write a balanced molecular equation for the reaction with HCl and calculate the amount of acid that reacted with the sample.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the mass percentage of calcium carbonate.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict the dry CO2 volume from the sample. The collected volume was only 168 cubic centimetres. Explain a possible low gas result that does not invalidate the titration.

steps.text: $\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)+2HCl(aq)\rightarrow CaCl_2(aq)+CO_2(g)+H_2O(l)}$.
Initial acid $=0.02500$ mol; excess acid $=0.02000(0.5000)=0.01000$ mol.
Acid consumed $=0.01500$ mol.
Mass $=0.750675$ g; percentage $=75.1\%$.
The 2:1 acid-to-carbonate ratio must be used; treating it as 1:1 would give an impossible mass greater than the sample mass.
Predicted volume 186 cubic centimetres.
Some carbon dioxide may dissolve in the collection liquid or escape through a leak; the acid consumption can still be measured correctly after carbon dioxide is removed.

title: Building a cell from displacement evidence
stem:
Experiments show that Mg displaces Zn from Zn2+(aq), Zn displaces Cu from Cu2+(aq), and Cu does not displace Zn from Zn2+(aq). A cell is constructed from Mg/Mg2+ and Cu2+/Cu half-cells as shown. No electrode-potential values are supplied or needed. Use $M(\mathrm{Mg})=24.31$ and $M(\mathrm{Cu})=63.55\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the evidence to identify the anode and cathode, state their signs during discharge, and write their half-equations.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain the directions of electron movement in the wire and ion movement in the salt bridge.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The magnesium electrode loses 0.4862 g. Assuming only the stated reactions, find the copper mass gained and explain why electrons do not carry current through the salt bridge.

steps.text: Mg is more easily oxidized than Zn, which is more easily oxidized than Cu; Mg is the negative anode and Cu the positive cathode.
Anode: $\mathrm{Mg(s)\rightarrow Mg^{2+}(aq)+2e^-}$.
Cathode: $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)+2e^-\rightarrow Cu(s)}$.
Electrons flow from the magnesium electrode to the copper electrode through the external wire.
Nitrate ions move toward the magnesium half-cell to balance accumulating magnesium ions.
Potassium ions move toward the copper half-cell to replace positive charge lost as copper ions are reduced.
$n(Mg)=0.4862/24.31=0.02000$ mol; the Cu:Mg molar ratio is 1:1.
Copper gained $=0.02000(63.55)=1.27$ g, using an unrounded mass of 1.271 g.
The bridge conducts by movement of ions; free electrons are carried by the metal circuit, not by the aqueous bridge.

title: Reversing a rechargeable cell without changing the chemistry
stem:
During discharge, the cell follows these half-equations: $\mathrm{Pb(s)+SO_4^{2-}(aq)\rightarrow PbSO_4(s)+2e^-}$ and $\mathrm{PbO_2(s)+SO_4^{2-}(aq)+4H^+(aq)+2e^-\rightarrow PbSO_4(s)+2H_2O(l)}$. Both electrode materials contact the same well-mixed electrolyte. Treat its volume as constant.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Combine the half-equations and identify which original electrode is oxidized during discharge.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Write the half-equation that occurs at the lead-metal plate during charging and identify its role then.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Discharge converts 0.0100 mol of PbO2. Initially the electrolyte contains 0.0500 mol of sulfuric acid, expressed as its formal amount. Find the remaining formal amount and explain the trend in acid concentration.

steps.text: Add the half-equations and cancel the two electrons.
$\mathrm{Pb+PbO_2+2SO_4^{2-}+4H^+\rightarrow 2PbSO_4+2H_2O}$, with states as given.
The lead metal electrode is oxidized: Pb goes from oxidation state 0 to +2.
Charging reverses the discharge conversion at this plate.
$\mathrm{PbSO_4(s)+2e^-\rightarrow Pb(s)+SO_4^{2-}(aq)}$.
The plate is the cathode during charging because reduction occurs there; an external electrical supply is required.
Each mole of PbO2 consumes 4 mol H+ and 2 mol sulfate, equivalent to 2 mol H2SO4.
Formal acid remaining $=0.0500-2(0.0100)=0.0300$ mol.
Acid is consumed on discharge, so its formal concentration falls at constant volume; this statement does not assume that both acid protons are fully dissociated.

title: Why melting changes the products of an ionic conductor
stem:
Pure MgCl2 is electrolysed using inert electrodes at 720 degrees Celsius, where both the electrolyte and magnesium product are liquid. There is no water. The same apparatus is first tested with solid MgCl2 and then with the melt. No current-time calculation is required.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain the difference in conduction before and after melting, and identify the charge carriers in the melt and the leads.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Write both electrode half-equations, with states, and identify the electrode signs.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A run decomposes 0.200 mol of MgCl2 completely. Determine both product amounts and explain why neither hydrogen nor oxygen is expected.

steps.text: In the solid the ions are held in fixed lattice positions and cannot migrate through the sample.
The melt contains mobile Mg2+ and Cl− ions, which carry current through the electrolyte.
Electrons carry current through the external metallic leads.
Negative cathode: $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}(l)+2e^-\rightarrow Mg(l)}$.
Positive anode: $\mathrm{2Cl^-(l)\rightarrow Cl_2(g)+2e^-}$.
Reduction occurs at the cathode and oxidation at the anode; the power supply drives the non-spontaneous overall change.

title: Choosing an apparatus to stop oxidation at the right stage
stem:
A primary alcohol, ethanol, can be oxidized first to an aldehyde and then to a carboxylic acid. The two apparatus arrangements are shown. Oxidation conditions and a suitable oxidizing agent are provided; the reagent’s identity need not be recalled. The aldehyde is more volatile than the alcohol and aqueous reaction mixture. The receiver in Y is cooled in an ice bath because ethanal boils near 20°C.

Reflux returns condensed volatile material to the flask, allowing prolonged heating and further oxidation without losing reactants.

A tertiary alcohol lacks a hydrogen on the carbon bearing the hydroxy group and is not oxidized under these same conditions without carbon–carbon bond cleavage.

title: The acidity controls a redox titration’s stoichiometry
stem:
A $25.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ Fe2+(aq) sample consumes $18.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.02000\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ MnO4− in strongly acidic solution. The intended manganese half-equation is $\mathrm{MnO_4^-+8H^++5e^-\rightarrow Mn^{2+}+4H_2O}$. If insufficient acid is present, a brown MnO2 solid may instead form by $\mathrm{MnO_4^-+4H^++3e^-\rightarrow MnO_2+2H_2O}$. These are the only manganese pathways to consider.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the iron half-equation and the overall ionic equation for the intended titration.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the concentration of Fe2+ in the sample using the intended reaction.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the significance of a brown solid and the direction of bias if the entire titrant is incorrectly treated as reacting by the five-electron pathway.

steps.text: $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}\rightarrow Fe^{3+}+e^-}$.
Multiply the iron half-equation by five and cancel electrons.
$\mathrm{MnO_4^-+8H^++5Fe^{2+}\rightarrow Mn^{2+}+4H_2O+5Fe^{3+}}$.
Brown MnO2 indicates that at least some permanganate has followed the three-electron pathway.
Each such mole of permanganate oxidizes only three moles of Fe2+, rather than five.
Using five for all titrant moles therefore overestimates the amount and concentration of iron.

title: A chain reaction makes more product than one initiation event
stem:
Ethane and chlorine are exposed to ultraviolet light. The diagram shows electron movement during the initiation stage. Restrict the product mechanism to the first substitution of ethane. Radical dots must be shown where appropriate.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the type of bond fission and write the initiation equation. Explain the meaning of each arrowhead.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Write the two propagation equations and explain why the process is a chain.

parts.label: c

steps.text: The Cl–Cl bond undergoes homolytic fission.
$\mathrm{Cl_2\xrightarrow{UV}2Cl{\cdot}}$.
Each fish-hook arrow represents one electron from the bonding pair moving to one chlorine atom.
$\mathrm{Cl{\cdot}+CH_3CH_3\rightarrow HCl+CH_3CH_2{\cdot}}$.
$\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{\cdot}+Cl_2\rightarrow CH_3CH_2Cl+Cl{\cdot}}$.
A chlorine radical is regenerated after each two-step cycle and can initiate another cycle without another Cl2 photolysis event.
$\mathrm{2CH_3CH_2{\cdot}\rightarrow CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_3}$.
Two unpaired electrons pair to form the new carbon–carbon bond.
No radical product remains, so these two chains can no longer propagate.

stem:
A closed reaction initially contains 0.100 mol methane and sufficient chlorine. After partial UV chlorination, carbon-containing products are separated. Corrected peak areas are proportional to moles, with all carbon remaining in the four indicated one-carbon species: CH4 20.0%, CH3Cl 50.0%, CH2Cl2 25.0%, CHCl3 5.0%. title: Following electron pairs without inventing a free electron
stem:
Aqueous hydroxide reacts with bromoethane to form ethanol. The reactant diagram shows lone pairs on oxygen and the polarized C–Br bond. Describe electron-pair movement only; a named kinetic mechanism or rate equation is not required.

steps.text: $\mathrm{OH^-}$ is the nucleophile and the carbon bonded to Br is the electrophilic atom.

One arrow starts at an oxygen lone pair and ends at the carbon bonded to bromine.
The other starts in the C–Br bonding pair and ends at bromine, which receives both electrons.
Heterolytic fission transfers the complete bonding pair to Br, forming Br− rather than Br·.
One group replaces another at carbon; the carbon skeleton and carbon–carbon bond order are retained.
Both charge and atoms are conserved: total charge is −1 on each side and no isolated free electron appears in the equation.

stem:
A 0.300 mol mixture contains only ethene and ethane. In an inert non-aqueous solvent in the dark it reacts with 0.180 mol Br2, which is just enough to remove all the ethene; ethane does not react under these conditions. In a subsequent UV experiment, each remaining ethane molecule undergoes exactly one substitution. The two starting molecules are shown.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the dark-reaction equation, name its reaction type, and explain why ethene reacts.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the initial mole fractions of ethene and ethane.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Write the UV substitution equation for ethane and compare the amounts of HBr formed in the two experiments.

steps.text: $\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2+Br_2\rightarrow CH_2BrCH_2Br}$.
Electrophilic addition; the product is 1,2-dibromoethane.
The carbon–carbon double bond has high electron density and can donate an electron pair to an electrophile.
The dark reaction consumes one Br2 per ethene, so ethene amount is 0.180 mol.
Ethane amount is $0.300-0.180=0.120$ mol.
Mole fractions: ethene 0.600 and ethane 0.400.
$\mathrm{C_2H_6+Br_2\xrightarrow{UV}C_2H_5Br+HBr}$.
The dark ethene addition gives no HBr; single substitution of the remaining ethane gives 0.120 mol HBr.
Addition incorporates both bromine atoms into the organic product; substitution replaces H by Br and releases HBr.

title: A weak-acid approximation has a limited range
stem:
A monoprotic acid HA has $K_a=1.80\times10^{-5}$. For a $0.0400\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ solution, a student assumes $[HA]_{\rm eq}\approx c$ and obtains $[H^+]\approx\sqrt{K_ac}$. The graph shows this approximate prediction over a range where the approximation is useful. Water autoionization is negligible in the cases considered.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

Unless specified otherwise, use 298 K, $K_w=1.00\times10^{-14}$ and ideal dilute-solution assumptions.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the ionization equation and Ka expression, then find the predicted pH of the 0.0400 mol dm−3 solution.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Test the approximation using the percentage dissociation. Then repeat this check at 0.000400 mol dm−3, without solving a quadratic.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the gradient of the plotted relationship and why extending its straight line indefinitely would be physically unsound.

steps.text: $\mathrm{HA+H_2O\rightleftharpoons H_3O^++A^-}$; $K_a=[H^+][A^-]/[HA]$.
Use estimated fraction dissociated $[H^+]/c$ in each case.
At 0.0400 M the fraction is 2.12%; at 0.000400 M it is 21.2%.
The first small depletion is reasonable under a 5% criterion; the second is too large to regard [HA] as unchanged.
$pH\approx\frac12(pK_a-\log_{10}c)$.
Gradient is −0.5 for pH versus log10(c).
At sufficiently low concentration the assumed small dissociation fails, and eventually water autoionization also matters; the same straight-line approximation cannot be extrapolated without limit.

title: A weak base and its conjugate-acid salt
stem:
Ammonia has $K_b=1.80\times10^{-5}$. Compare separate $0.0800\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ solutions of NH3 and NH4Cl. Chloride has negligible acid–base activity. Use small-ionization approximations and verify them.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

Unless specified otherwise, use 298 K, $K_w=1.00\times10^{-14}$ and ideal dilute-solution assumptions.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate Ka for NH4+ and write the ammonium hydrolysis equation.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the pH of each solution and check the approximate fractional ionization in each.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why dissolving NH4Cl can lower pH although no HCl molecule is released.

steps.text: $\mathrm{NH_4^++H_2O\rightleftharpoons NH_3+H_3O^+}$.
For ammonia, $[OH^-]\approx\sqrt{K_bc}$, then $pOH=-\log[OH^-]$ and $pH=14-pOH$.
Ammonia pH $=11.079$; fractional ionization $=1.50\%$.
For ammonium, $[H^+]\approx\sqrt{K_ac}$.
NH4Cl pH $=5.176$; fractional ionization $=0.00833\%$, so both are small.
NH4+ donates a proton to water in an equilibrium reaction.
The chloride ion is a spectator; acidity arises from the conjugate acid of the weak base.
A salt dissociates into its ions; producing free HCl molecules is neither necessary nor the stated aqueous process.

title: Adjusting a buffer by consuming conjugate base
stem:
A buffer is made with 0.0100 mol ethanoic acid HA and 0.0150 mol sodium ethanoate A− in a total volume of 250 cubic centimetres. The acid has pKa 4.76. An added small amount of strong acid reacts essentially completely with A−. Use the acid equilibrium expression; no quadratic solution is required.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

Unless specified otherwise, use 298 K, $K_w=1.00\times10^{-14}$ and ideal dilute-solution assumptions.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Derive the concentration-ratio form for pH and find the initial buffer pH.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the volume of 1.00 mol dm−3 HCl needed to change the pH to 4.76, assuming volumes are additive.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Write the buffer’s reaction with added HCl and explain why a comparable amount of pure strong acid would not itself make an acidic buffer.

steps.text: From $K_a=[H^+][A^-]/[HA]$, rearrange to $[H^+]=K_a[HA]/[A^-]$.
Target pH = pKa requires equal acid and conjugate-base amounts; after x mol HCl these are $0.0100+x$ and $0.0150-x$.
$x=0.00250$ mol, requiring 2.50 cubic centimetres HCl.
The common final volume cancels from the concentration ratio; it must not be applied to only one component.
$\mathrm{CH_3COO^-+H^+\rightarrow CH_3COOH}$.
The buffer contains appreciable amounts of a weak acid and its conjugate base, allowing added acid or base to be consumed.
A strong acid is essentially fully dissociated and does not provide a comparable reservoir of a weak acid/conjugate-base pair.

title: Equal initial pH does not mean equal buffer capacity
stem:
Buffer P contains 0.0200 mol HA and 0.0100 mol A− in 200 cubic centimetres; pKa(HA) = 4.00. Buffer Q is prepared by diluting an identical complete portion to 2.00 dm3. Separate 20.0 cubic centimetre aliquots of P and Q each receive 1.00 cubic centimetre of 1.50 mol dm−3 NaOH. Assume quantitative neutralization before any weak equilibrium calculation.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

Unless specified otherwise, use 298 K, $K_w=1.00\times10^{-14}$ and ideal dilute-solution assumptions.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the common initial pH and explain why the dilution scarcely changes it.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the final pH after adding NaOH to the P aliquot.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the final pH for the Q aliquot and explain the difference from P.

steps.text: Both initial pH values are approximately 3.699.
Dilution changes both component concentrations by the same factor, so their ratio is unchanged, provided the buffer approximation remains valid.
The aliquot initially has 0.00200 mol HA and 0.00100 mol A−; hydroxide added is 0.00150 mol.
After reaction, HA = 0.000500 mol and A− = 0.00250 mol.
Q’s aliquot initially has only 0.000200 mol HA; 0.00130 mol OH− therefore remains in 0.0210 dm3.
pH $=12.792$, strongly basic.
Equal initial ratios give equal starting pH, but Q has much less neutralizing acid per aliquot, so the same added hydroxide exhausts its buffer component.

title: Reading a weak-acid titration before choosing an indicator
stem:
A $25.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ monoprotic weak-acid sample is titrated with $0.100\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ NaOH. Equivalence occurs at $25.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ and the pH at half-equivalence is 4.80. Candidate indicators change colour over pH 3.1–4.4 and 8.2–10.0. Use small-ionization approximations where needed.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

Unless specified otherwise, use 298 K, $K_w=1.00\times10^{-14}$ and ideal dilute-solution assumptions.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

parts.label: c

steps.text: At equivalence, acid amount is $0.100(0.0250)=0.00250$ mol.
Acid concentration $=0.100\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$; $K_a=10^{-4.80}=1.58\times10^{-5}$.
At half-equivalence the amounts of HA and A− are equal, so the equilibrium expression gives [H+] = Ka and pH = pKa.
$\mathrm{A^-+H_2O\rightleftharpoons HA+OH^-}$.
Equivalence pH $=8.749$.
Use the indicator with range 8.2–10.0, matching the steep basic equivalence region.
Water does not change the amount of acid, so equivalence still requires 25.0 cubic centimetres of NaOH.
The pH curve changes with dilution, but the stoichiometric amount required for equivalence does not.

title: A weak-base titration with an acidic equivalence point
stem:
A 20.0 cubic centimetre sample of a monofunctional weak base B, concentration 0.0800 mol dm−3, is titrated with 0.100 mol dm−3 HCl. The base has pKb 4.30. Treat B/BH+ as the only weak conjugate system.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

Unless specified otherwise, use 298 K, $K_w=1.00\times10^{-14}$ and ideal dilute-solution assumptions.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the equivalence volume and the pH at half-equivalence.

parts.label: b

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why the equivalence solution is acidic. Choose between indicators with ranges 4.4–6.2 and 8.2–10.0, and distinguish an indicator end point from equivalence.

steps.text: Base amount $=0.0800(0.0200)=0.00160$ mol, giving 16.0 cubic centimetres acid at equivalence.
At half-equivalence, [B] = [BH+], so pOH = pKb = 4.30.
Half-equivalence is at 8.00 cubic centimetres and pH = 9.700.
$[H^+]\approx\sqrt{K_a[BH^+]}$.
Equivalence pH $=5.526$.
$\mathrm{BH^++H_2O\rightleftharpoons B+H_3O^+}$ makes the solution acidic.
The 4.4–6.2 indicator is more suitable.
Equivalence is the stoichiometric acid/base balance; the observed colour end point occurs over an indicator equilibrium range and need not coincide exactly.

title: Measuring an indicator equilibrium by absorbance
stem:
An indicator obeys $\mathrm{HInd(aq)\rightleftharpoons H^+(aq)+Ind^-(aq)}$ with pKa 5.50. At a chosen wavelength, only HInd absorbs appreciably and absorbance is proportional to its concentration. At the same total indicator concentration and path length, completely protonated indicator has absorbance 0.500; an unknown buffered sample has absorbance 0.100. The spectra illustrate the two forms; no particular molecular structure is assumed.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

Unless specified otherwise, use 298 K, $K_w=1.00\times10^{-14}$ and ideal dilute-solution assumptions.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the indicator Ka expression and find the fractions of indicator present as HInd and Ind−.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the sample pH and explain which component is favoured as pH increases.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Show why the colour transition is spread over a pH interval rather than occurring at one exact pH. Find the pH values for concentration ratios 0.10 and 10.0.

steps.text: The protonated fraction is $0.100/0.500=0.200$.
Fractions are 0.200 HInd and 0.800 Ind−.
Higher pH means lower [H+], shifting the indicator equilibrium toward Ind−.
Use pH = pKa + log(conjugate ratio).
The ratios 0.10 and 10.0 give pH 4.500 and 6.500, respectively.
Both coloured forms coexist through the equilibrium range; the eye detects a change in their relative contributions, not an instantaneous conversion at equivalence.

title: Electron-pair donation without a proton transfer
stem:
BF3 reacts with NH3 to form a 1:1 adduct. The diagram shows their Lewis formulas. In a separate ligand-exchange system, a Co(III) complex contains four neutral NH3 ligands and two Cl− ligands. A chloride ligand is replaced by a fifth ammonia ligand; the coordination number remains six.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the Lewis acid and Lewis base in the BF3/NH3 reaction, and describe the origin and destination of the donated electron pair.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe or draw the adduct’s N–B bond and determine the formal charges on N and B in its Lewis representation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the charges of the original cobalt complex and the complex after ligand exchange. Write the balanced ligand-exchange equation.

steps.text: BF3 is the Lewis acid; NH3 is the Lewis base.
The lone pair on nitrogen is donated toward boron to form the N–B bond.
Boron begins with six electrons around it and can accept a pair; no proton transfer is necessary.
Adduct $\mathrm{H_3N\rightarrow BF_3}$ has four bonds around both N and B.
Nitrogen has formal charge +1; boron −1; the whole adduct is neutral.
After formation the coordinate bond is an ordinary shared-pair covalent bond; its donated origin does not make its electrons permanently distinguishable.
For Co(III), four NH3 and two Cl− give $+3+0-2=+1$; five NH3 and one Cl− give +2.
$\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]^++NH_3\rightleftharpoons[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]^{2+}+Cl^-}$.
One anionic ligand leaves as Cl−, balancing the increased complex charge while six donor ligands remain coordinated.

title: The voltmeter sign depends on the leads, not the chemistry
stem:
The left half-cell is the standard hydrogen electrode, using platinum, H2 at 100 kPa and $[H^+]=1.00\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$. The right half-cell is Cu2+/Cu at $[Cu^{2+}]=1.00\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$. Both are at 298 K. With the red voltmeter lead on Cu and the black lead on Pt, the reading is +0.340 V. The standard hydrogen reduction potential is defined as 0.000 V.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce the standard reduction potential of Cu2+/Cu and identify the spontaneous electrode reactions.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: State the electron direction and explain what changes if only the voltmeter leads are exchanged.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why each of the three specified standard-state conditions matters and why the salt bridge cannot be replaced by a dry insulating tube.

steps.text: A positive reading with the red lead on Cu identifies Cu as the higher-potential electrode in this discharge cell.
$E^\circ(Cu^{2+}/Cu)=+0.340$ V; $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}+2e^-\rightarrow Cu}$ at the cathode.
At Pt, $\mathrm{H_2\rightarrow2H^++2e^-}$; Pt is an inert electron conductor.
Electrons in the external circuit move from the hydrogen electrode toward copper.
The voltmeter reading changes to −0.340 V.
Exchanging measuring leads reverses the displayed potential difference, but does not reverse the spontaneous chemical reaction or reassign the physical anode/cathode.
Electrode potentials depend on aqueous composition, gas pressure and temperature; the standard comparison fixes these conditions.
A conducting salt bridge permits ion migration to maintain bulk electrical neutrality as redox occurs.
A dry insulating tube provides no ionic path, so charge separation would halt sustained current.

title: Scaling a redox equation does not scale its voltage
stem:
Use these standard reduction potentials: $\mathrm{Sn^{4+}(aq)+2e^-\rightleftharpoons Sn^{2+}(aq)}$, +0.150 V; $\mathrm{I_2(s)+2e^-\rightleftharpoons2I^-(aq)}$, +0.540 V. In the model cell, solid iodine is in contact with the iodide solution and inert electrodes provide electrical contact. Take $F=96500\ \mathrm{C\,mol^{-1}}$.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the spontaneous overall reaction and identify the oxidizing and reducing agents.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the standard cell potential and the standard Gibbs energy change per mole of the equation as written.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student doubles every coefficient and reports a cell potential of 0.780 V. Correct this claim, give the corresponding Gibbs energy change, and distinguish spontaneity from reaction speed.

steps.text: The more positive reduction potential selects iodine reduction; reverse the tin half-equation.
$\mathrm{Sn^{2+}+I_2\rightarrow Sn^{4+}+2I^-}$.
I2 is the oxidizing agent; Sn2+ is the reducing agent.
$E^\circ_{\rm cell}=0.540-0.150$; two moles of electrons are transferred.
$E^\circ_{\rm cell}=+0.390$ V.
Cell potential is an intensive quantity, so it remains +0.390 V.
The doubled reaction transfers 4 mol electrons and has Gibbs energy change −151 kJ per mole of the doubled equation, using an unrounded value of −150.54 kJ.
A negative standard Gibbs energy change establishes thermodynamic favourability under standard conditions, not a fast rate; an activation barrier can still slow the reaction.

title: The same ion can be oxidized and reduced
stem:
The standard reduction potentials are $\mathrm{Cu^++e^-\rightleftharpoons Cu(s)}$, +0.520 V, and $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}+e^-\rightleftharpoons Cu^+}$, +0.150 V. Consider only these couples under standard conditions. Use $F=96500\ \mathrm{C\,mol^{-1}}$.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Construct the disproportionation reaction of Cu+ and explain its classification.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate its standard cell potential and Gibbs energy change, showing the number of electrons transferred per equation.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: If 0.0400 mol of Cu+ disproportionates completely, find both product amounts. Explain why using n = 2 in the Gibbs equation would double-count the electron transfer.

steps.text: $\mathrm{2Cu^+\rightarrow Cu^{2+}+Cu(s)}$.
One Cu+ loses an electron to become Cu2+ while another gains an electron to become Cu metal.
The same reactant species is therefore both oxidized and reduced.
Cathodic Cu+/Cu is +0.520 V; the reversed Cu2+/Cu+ step supplies oxidation, so $E^\circ=0.520-0.150$.
Cell potential is +0.370 V; one mole of electrons is transferred per 2 mol of Cu+ consumed.
The stoichiometric coefficients give one mole of each product from two moles of Cu+.
0.0200 mol Cu2+ and 0.0200 mol Cu(s).
The electron lost by one Cu+ is the same electron gained by the other; it is counted once as transferred, rather than once at each electrode.

title: An electrode can replenish the electrolyte or consume water
stem:
An aqueous copper(II) sulfate electrolyte is electrolysed with either two inert electrodes or a copper anode and an inert cathode. Copper deposits at the cathode in both runs. The inert anode releases oxygen; the copper anode instead dissolves, with no gas. Treat electrolyte volume as constant and assume only the observed electrode processes. Each run deposits 0.0200 mol Cu from an initial 0.100 mol Cu2+ in 0.100 dm3.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the cathode half-equation and the two possible anode half-equations, with states.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: For the inert-anode run, find the final Cu2+ concentration, oxygen amount and amount of H+ generated.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the different copper-ion trend for the copper-anode run, and compare the anode and cathode copper mass changes.

steps.text: Cathode: $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)+2e^-\rightarrow Cu(s)}$.
Inert anode: $\mathrm{2H_2O(l)\rightarrow O_2(g)+4H^+(aq)+4e^-}$.
Copper anode: $\mathrm{Cu(s)\rightarrow Cu^{2+}(aq)+2e^-}$.
Two moles of deposited copper require four moles of electrons, corresponding to one mole O2 and four moles H+.
Final Cu2+ is 0.0800 mol in 0.100 dm3, giving 0.800 mol dm−3.
O2 produced = 0.0100 mol; H+ generated = 0.0400 mol.
Anode dissolution produces the same amount of Cu2+ that the cathode consumes, so its total amount and concentration remain approximately unchanged.
The anode loses the same copper mass that the cathode gains, assuming only these copper processes.
The electrode material changes the available oxidation reaction; calling every anode inert would miss this material balance.

title: A plating mass deficit reveals a competing reduction
stem:
A nickel anode supplies Ni2+ to an electroplating bath while a conducting object is coated at the other electrode. The anode loses 0.900 g Ni; the object gains only 0.810 g Ni. Assume all anode loss forms Ni2+, all object mass gain is Ni, and the remaining electron transfer produces H2 by $\mathrm{2H^++2e^-\rightarrow H_2}$. Use $M(Ni)=58.69\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$. No current-time calculation is needed.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the electrode connection needed for the object and write both nickel half-equations.

parts.label: b

steps.text: The object must be the negative cathode; nickel reduction deposits the coating there.

Depositing fraction $=0.810/0.900=0.900$, or 90.0%.
The difference in nickel-equivalent moles corresponds to 2 electron moles per mole; producing one H2 also requires 2 electron moles.
A competing reduction diverts electrons away from metal deposition, leaving some newly formed Ni2+ in solution.

title: Gas ratios distinguish brine and water electrolysis
stem:
Concentrated aqueous NaCl is electrolysed in separated compartments with inert electrodes. Under the stated operating conditions the observed anode product is Cl2 and the cathode product is H2; a membrane prevents chlorine contacting the cathodic alkaline solution. In a separate dilute solution under conditions favouring water oxidation, the observed gases are O2 and H2. Product identities are supplied, so no overpotential or Nernst calculation is required.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the half-equations for the concentrated-brine run and identify the origin of hydrogen.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: The brine run produces 0.0120 mol Cl2. Find the hydrogen amount and the pH if the generated hydroxide is retained in a final cathode-solution volume of 0.200 dm3.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: For the dilute water-oxidation run, write an anode equation and deduce the H2:O2 gas-volume ratio at equal temperature and pressure. Explain why the two experiments have different gas ratios.

steps.text: Anode: $\mathrm{2Cl^-(aq)\rightarrow Cl_2(g)+2e^-}$.
Cathode: $\mathrm{2H_2O(l)+2e^-\rightarrow H_2(g)+2OH^-(aq)}$.
Hydrogen comes from water reduction; sodium ions remain aqueous rather than being deposited as sodium metal.
Equal two-electron gas steps give 0.0120 mol H2 and 0.0240 mol OH−.
$\mathrm{2H_2O\rightarrow O_2+4H^++4e^-}$ at the anode.
H2:O2 is 2:1, whereas H2:Cl2 in the concentrated-brine run is 1:1.
One O2 releases four electrons but one H2 consumes only two; one Cl2 releases two. The ratios follow electron balance, not the initial salt formula alone.

title: A substitution builds one extra carbon into the chain
stem:
1-Bromopropane reacts with cyanide, CN−, by the concerted SN2 pathway. Cyanide attacks through its carbon atom. The diagram gives a condensed ethyl group attached to the electrophilic CH2 centre and shows the cyanide lone pair. Ignore competing pathways and solvent effects.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the substitution equation and give the product’s carbon skeleton and functional-group name.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe the two curly arrows, the approach direction and whether a free carbocation is an intermediate.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain the distinction between a transition state and an intermediate, and account for all charges in the net equation.

steps.text: $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2Br+CN^-\rightarrow CH_3CH_2CH_2CN+Br^-}$.
The product has four carbons in its principal chain and is butanenitrile.
Cyanide contributes a carbon atom; replacing Br by CN does not leave the original carbon count unchanged.
The donor arrow begins at cyanide’s carbon lone pair and ends at the carbon bearing Br.
The C–Br bonding pair moves to Br; attack is from the side opposite the C–Br bond.
Bond formation and bond breaking occur in one concerted step; there is a transition state, not a separately formed carbocation intermediate.
A transition state is a maximum-energy arrangement along the reaction coordinate, not an isolable species occupying an energy minimum.
An intermediate would be a discrete species formed in one step and consumed in another; that is not the stated SN2 path.
The total −1 charge moves from the nucleophile to bromide; the nitrile product is neutral and no free electron is released.

title: A tertiary substitution passes through an oxonium ion
stem:
2-Chloro-2-methylpropane reacts with water by an SN1 pathway. A carbocation is formed before water attacks. The final organic product is 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Include the proton-transfer step needed after water attack; do not use hydroxide as the attacking species in this specified mechanism.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the first electron-pair movement and draw or describe the carbocation, including its charge and carbon bonding.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain water attack and identify the immediate product, including the oxygen charge.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Write the final proton-transfer step and the overall equation with water. Explain why omitting this final step gives the wrong final organic charge.

steps.text: The C–Cl bonding pair moves to chlorine, so the C–Cl bond breaks heterolytically.
$\mathrm{(CH_3)_3CCl\rightarrow (CH_3)_3C^++Cl^-}$.
The positively charged central carbon has three sigma bonds and an empty orbital; it is approximately trigonal planar.
A lone pair on the water oxygen is donated to the carbocation carbon.
$\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C^++H_2O\rightarrow (CH_3)_3COH_2^+}$.
The attacking oxygen now has three bonds and one lone pair, giving an oxonium ion with formal charge +1.
$\mathrm{(CH_3)_3COH_2^++H_2O\rightarrow (CH_3)_3COH+H_3O^+}$.
Overall: $\mathrm{(CH_3)_3CCl+2H_2O\rightarrow (CH_3)_3COH+H_3O^++Cl^-}$.
Loss of a proton returns the alcohol oxygen to two bonds and two lone pairs; the isolated alcohol is neutral, not an oxonium ion.

title: Recognizing inversion from three-dimensional structures
stem:
An optically active sample of 2-bromobutane undergoes substitution with hydroxide. For this question the reaction is known to follow only an SN2 pathway; no inference from solvent or rate data is required. The reactant and candidate alcohol products P and Q are shown with the same two carbon groups held in the plane. A solid wedge points towards the observer and a hashed wedge points away. No R/S descriptors are needed.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why P represents retention in this comparison and why optical activity alone does not identify the reaction mechanism.

parts.label: c

steps.text: Q is consistent with SN2 inversion.
The entering hydroxy group approaches from the side opposite the departing C–Br bond.
With the two in-plane carbon groups held fixed, the positions of H and the entering group reverse their towards/away arrangement.
P replaces Br by OH in the same away-pointing position while H remains towards the observer, retaining the arrangement shown.
Optical activity establishes a non-racemic chiral sample, not a unique pathway for every possible reaction.
Secondary halogenoalkanes can follow different substitution pathways; the pure SN2 condition is an explicit premise here.
$\mathrm{CH_3CHBrCH_2CH_3+OH^-\rightarrow CH_3CHOHCH_2CH_3+Br^-}$.
Oxygen donates a lone pair to make C–O while retaining its O–H bond.
The alcohol oxygen has two bonds and two lone pairs and is neutral; the overall −1 charge is carried by bromide.

title: The leaving-group comparison must keep the carbon skeleton fixed
stem:
Comparable hydrolysis experiments use CH3CH2Cl, CH3CH2Br and CH3CH2I at the same concentration, temperature and solvent composition. The plotted fractions reacted are experimental models for this comparison, not a request to infer rate laws. Their carbon–halogen bond enthalpies are 338, 276 and 238 kJ mol−1 respectively. A separately added AgNO3 test detects halide released after a fixed reaction period.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Rank the hydrolysis rates from the plots and explain the trend using leaving-group evidence.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Write the net hydrolysis equation for the bromide and the ionic equation for detecting its released halide.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why these data cannot establish a solvent effect or distinguish SN1 from SN2 by themselves.

steps.text: CH3CH2I reacts fastest, then CH3CH2Br, then CH3CH2Cl.
The C–I bond is the weakest of the supplied set and is broken more readily in the controlled comparison.
I− is a better leaving group than Br−, which is better than Cl−; all three substrates share the same carbon structure, making the comparison meaningful.
$\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Br+OH^-\rightarrow CH_3CH_2OH+Br^-}$.
$\mathrm{Ag^++Br^-\rightarrow AgBr(s)}$.
The precipitate detects halide released into solution; it is not evidence that silver directly replaces bromine on the organic molecule.
The solvent is held constant, so the experiment contains no controlled comparison between solvents.
The displayed extent curves and bond data do not by themselves specify a complete rate law or reveal an intermediate.
Changing several substrate features simultaneously would confound the leaving-group comparison; the fixed ethyl skeleton avoids that error.

title: Tracing deuterium through an unsymmetrical addition
stem:
Propene reacts with DBr, where D is hydrogen-2. Treat D+ chemically as H+ for this mechanism and ignore isotope effects. Two carbocation pathways are possible. No rearrangement occurs. The more stable carbocation pathway gives the major product.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the first pair of curly arrows and identify the more stable carbocation, including the location of D.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the nucleophile in the second step and draw or give the condensed formula of the major organic product.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Give the minor product and explain how both products preserve carbon valence four while retaining all six original ordinary hydrogen atoms.

steps.text: A pair from the C=C bond is donated to D; the D–Br bonding pair moves to Br.
The more stable intermediate is $\mathrm{CH_3C^+(H)CH_2D}$, with D on the terminal carbon.
Its positive carbon is secondary; adding D to the middle carbon instead would leave a less stable primary carbocation at the end.
Br− attacks by donating a bromide lone pair to the positively charged carbon.
Major product $\mathrm{CH_3CH(Br)CH_2D}$.
The more substituted carbocation is stabilized by electron donation from adjacent alkyl groups; the reasoning concerns the intermediate, rather than an unsupported preference for a product name.
Minor product $\mathrm{CH_3CH(D)CH_2Br}$.
In each pathway the carbon receiving D gains one sigma bond as the double bond becomes a single bond; carbon still has total bond order four.
The original six ordinary hydrogens remain, and D plus Br are added across the former double bond; no hydrogen is displaced in this addition.

title: The water oxygen enters while the acid catalyst returns
stem:
Ethene is hydrated in an acidic aqueous mixture. The reactive water is enriched in oxygen-18; treat its oxygen as 18O for tracing and ignore isotope exchange after product formation. Hydronium provides a proton in the first step. The final alcohol is neutral. No special acid reagent or electrophile-generation recipe is required.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the first electron-pair movements and write the carbocation-forming equation.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain attack by labelled water and give the charged intermediate and neutral organic product, retaining the oxygen label.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Write the proton-transfer step in words or an equation, and explain which species is a catalyst and which supplies the product oxygen.

steps.text: A C=C electron pair moves toward a proton on H3O+.
The electrons in that O–H bond move back onto oxygen, so the proton donor becomes water.
$\mathrm{C_2H_4+H_3O^+\rightarrow C_2H_5^++H_2O}$.
A lone pair on labelled water oxygen is donated to the carbocation carbon.
Intermediate $\mathrm{C_2H_5{}^{18}OH_2^+}$; neutral product $\mathrm{C_2H_5{}^{18}OH}$.
Oxygen has three bonds and +1 formal charge in the intermediate, then two bonds and no charge after deprotonation.
A water molecule accepts a proton from the protonated alcohol, producing neutral labelled ethanol and regenerating H3O+.
Hydronium is regenerated, so it is the acid catalyst rather than a net reactant.
The nucleophilic labelled water supplies the alcohol oxygen; the hydronium oxygen from the first step is not transferred into the carbon skeleton in this traced pathway.

title: Restoring aromaticity completes electrophilic substitution
stem:
Benzene reacts with a supplied nitronium electrophile, $E^+=\mathrm{NO_2^+}$. The diagram shows the initial electron-pair attack. Formation of the electrophile is outside this question. A neutral base B with an available lone pair removes a proton from the sigma complex.

Give non-exact numerical answers to three significant figures; report pH values to three decimal places unless stated otherwise.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the electron-pair origin in the first step and the bonding and charge of the sigma complex.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe the two electron-pair movements during proton removal and state both products of that step.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Write the net reaction for E+ = NO2+ and explain why the overall process is substitution rather than addition.

steps.text: An electron pair from a benzene carbon–carbon pi bond is donated to E+ to form a C–E sigma bond.
The attacked carbon temporarily has four sigma bonds: two ring bonds, H and E; it is no longer part of a continuous six-electron aromatic ring.
The intermediate has overall charge +1, delocalized over the remaining conjugated part of the ring; it is not the final neutral product.
A base lone pair moves toward the H attached to the carbon bearing E.
The C–H bonding pair returns to the ring to form the missing pi bond, restoring aromaticity.
Products are substituted benzene, C6H5E, and BH+; the proton leaves, not a neutral H atom or hydride.
$\mathrm{C_6H_6+NO_2^+\rightarrow C_6H_5NO_2+H^+}$, with the proton accepted by B in the actual final step.
One ring H is replaced by NO2 and the aromatic pi system is restored.
Stopping at an addition-like sigma complex would retain the positive, non-aromatic intermediate instead of completing the favourable aromatic restoration.
